correctness.rationale: Pass applies to the repaired RESULT.md and SLOGAN.txt, not the standalone literal parameter statement in the frozen result. The frozen inequality (4d+2)p<1 does not specify positive decay. At p=0 the formula has p^(−1), and CG on the identity stops at one step at zero tolerance rather than following the stated law. Negative p is not fixed by excluding the singular point: for example p=−1 under the literal inequality gives a non-probability density on the asserted support [1,∞), whereas (n/j)^p lies in (0,1]. The repaired theorem specifies 0<p<1/(4d+2), the intended decay regime. Independently checked its proof: after scaling the spectral variable, the common normalization of Haar coordinates cancels and the weights are Y_{j,n}E_j with independent mean-one exponentials (real model: chi-squares with one degree of freedom). The real minimizer suffices since imaginary coefficients add nonnegative energy with zero constraint at the origin. Under x=1/y, the normalization r(0)=1 makes x^d r(1/x) monic and the weight becomes x^(p^(−1)−2d−2). The shifted Jacobi leading coefficient is binom(p^(−1)−2,d), and its squared norm before making it monic is 1/(p^(−1)−1); the density prefactor cancels this norm, giving F_d. A mesh-vs-integral bound O(n^(ap−1)) on the a-th raw mean is o(n^(−1/2)) for ap<1/2; the largest centered coefficient in each √n-scaled linear combination is O(n^((2d+1)p−1/2)), and the quadratic covariances tend to 1/(1−(a+b)p). Bounded total coefficient squares and a vanishing largest coefficient imply Lindeberg by integrability of the squared centered weights. The limiting Gram block is positive definite, so the optimizing polynomial coefficients and the Schur-complement quotient are smooth near the limit. Differentiating the optimized quotient gives (1−p)y(r(y)^2−F_d) at a grid point; its squared integral against t on (0,1] changes to (1−p) times the integral of y(r²−F_d)² against ν_p. It is positive because the degree-d polynomial is nonconstant, and finite since the tail exponent is 4d+1−1/p<−1. A variance-two raw weight multiplies the covariance and the final variance by two. Since (2d+3)p<1, a weighted law of large numbers applies to degree d+1 as well (integrable deterministic means and maximal unscaled weight tending to zero). The binomial ratio gives F_{d−1}>F_d>F_{d+1}, with F_0=1. Monotonicity of the actual errors then leaves only steps d and d+1 with high probability, and continuity and symmetry of the nondegenerate limiting Gaussian give the two equal masses. No claim at the variance boundary, for growing degree, or in finite precision was accepted.
